candidates.title: Jiangnan Shipyard wins BV approval for electric-propelled ammonia carrier
candidates.excerpt: Jiangnan Shipyard has received Approval in Principle (AiP) from Bureau Veritas for a new electric-propelled Very Large Ammonia Carrier (VLAC). The vessel concept combines ammonia-fueled power generation with batteries, fuel cells and wind-assisted propulsion. Jiangnan Shipyard, a subsidiary of China State Shipbuilding Corporation (CSSC), developed the design in-house. VLAC combines three power sources The vessel features a medium-voltage DC hybrid electric propulsion system. It integrates three power sources: ammonia-fueled generators, an ammonia fuel cell system and containerized battery energy storage. The design also features a forward accommodation arrangement. According to Bureau Veritas, the hybrid architecture is intended to improve operational efficiency. It also provides flexibility to integrate new energy technologies in the future. Four sails provide additional propulsion The VLAC design includes four foldable soft sails for wind-assisted propulsion. These will provide supplementary propulsion and help reduce the vessel’s overall energy consumption. Jiangnan’s concept therefore combines ammonia, electric propulsion, energy storage and wind power within a single vessel design. The shipyard has also designed the vessel with future upgrades in mind. Potential additions include more advanced batteries, onboard photovoltaic power generation and next-generation fuel cells.

The flip side is that the high sustained fuel prices — which NS expects to remain elevated for the rest of the year — will be a 2.5-point hit to the railroad’s operating ratio, Chief Financial Officer Jason Zampi says. Eventually the railroad’s fuel surcharge will catch up, but from a quarter-to-quarter basis fuel costs will be a headwind, he explains. The danger is that sustained high fuel prices will hurt consumer spending and sap demand, Elkins says. “We still see clear demand growth on the industrial side. candidates.excerpt: RALEIGH, N.C. — The North Carolina Railroad will invest up to $250,000 to support the construction of a new rail spur serving Atlantic Packagin’s warehouse expansion in Tabor City, N.C. Once operational, the facility is expected to receive and distribute at least 480 rail cars annually. candidates.excerpt: Few things match the thrill of standing trackside while an earth-shaking freight thunders past. candidates.title: Direct lending: What has (and hasn’t) changed
candidates.excerpt: Direct lending: What has (and hasn’t) changed Tyler Gately and Stuart Mathieson of Barings argue that, despite increased scrutiny of direct lending, the fundamentals that first attracted investors to the buoyant asset class remain intact. Private credit has attracted increasing attention in the past few years. As the market has grown in size and visibility, periods of uncertainty have drawn greater scrutiny to direct lending in particular, often fueled by headlines tied to isolated credit events, fundraising trends or shifts in capital flows. The attention is understandable. Direct lending today is significantly larger and more broadly followed than it was a decade ago. But while the market has evolved, many of the characteristics that initially attracted investors to the asset class remain intact. Understanding what has changed – and what has not – provides useful context for evaluating the opportunity set ahead. What hasn’t changed At its core, traditional middle market direct lending remains anchored by the same principles that have long defined the strategy: senior secured lending, contractual cash flows and a focus on downside protection. Most direct lending transactions continue to involve first lien loans to sponsor-backed middle market companies. candidates.title: FMC Judge Rejects Peloton’s $33.7 Million Demurrage Claim Against Flexport
candidates.excerpt: A Federal Maritime Commission administrative law judge has rejected Peloton Interactive’s bid to recover $33.7 million in detention, demurrage and related charges from Flexport. In an initial decision served September 9, Administrative Law Judge Mary Apostolakos Hervey found Peloton failed to prove that Flexport’s practices violated the Shipping Act or caused the losses it claimed. Flexport was found not liable for reparations. The ruling is the latest in a growing number of FMC decisions stemming from the pandemic-era supply chain crunch, when severe port congestion, equipment shortages and inland bottlenecks triggered a wave of disputes over detention and demurrage charges. Peloton filed the case in 2024, arguing that Flexport improperly assessed detention and demurrage on thousands of shipments during the pandemic-era supply chain crunch. The company said Flexport should have borne charges tied to issues including chassis shortages, port congestion and inland transportation delays.

This rule amends freight car draft arrangement and end-of-car cushioning unit (EOCC) regulations to make permanent relief currently provided by waiver. The amendments will allow a freight car to remain in service if the EOCC is operative and equipped with a unit condition indicator (UCI) that indicates a non-discharged EOCC. candidates.title: CN tests more yard shunting hybrid locomotives
candidates.excerpt: CN has widened its hybrid-electric locomotive programme from one pilot locomotive to a five-unit development track, moving the work from a single demonstrator into broader testing of repowered yard power. The Montreal-based Class I railroad said on 14 August 2026 that three locomotives are now being tested and that two more are being converted into hybrid-electric platforms with AC traction technology by the end of 2026. The programme is aimed at existing yard locomotives rather than new-build line-haul power, which keeps the focus on fuel use, idling, low-speed tractive effort and asset life in terminal operations. CN said its initial pilot achieved fuel-efficiency gains of up to 50%, fewer engine-related failures, higher horsepower and lower idling. Those are company-reported test results, not a network-wide performance figure. candidates.title: Europe tightens checks on freight railcars following the Gotthard accident
candidates.excerpt: Technical inspections of freight railcars in Europe are set to become much more frequent following the accident in the Gotthard Base Tunnel in 2023. The new measures, strongly championed by Switzerland, provide for checks based on the type of wheels after approximately 50,000–300,000 km, compared with intervals that could previously be as long as 660,000 km. The serious accident that occurred three years ago in the Gotthard Base Tunnel is changing the safety regulations for European rail freight transport. The authorities and the rail industry have agreed on harmonised measures involving more frequent inspections of railcars and, in particular, their wheels, after investigations into the derailment in August 2023 revealed the risk of cracks and fractures.
